questions.question: A cardiologist is consulted for a patient with chest pain. The word part cardi(o)- in the specialist's title tells you this doctor's specialty involves the:
questions.explanation: The case study breaks down cardiologist as cardi (heart) plus -logist (specialist): a heart specialist.

questions.question: A patient coughs up blood after a chest injury, a finding whose name contains the word part hem(o)-. That word part refers to:
questions.explanation: The case study states it directly: hemo means "blood," as in hemoptysis, coughing up blood.

questions.question: A hematology lab panel is ordered to check a patient's blood counts. Hemat(o)- is the combining form of the same root as hem(o)-, so hematology is the study of:
questions.explanation: Hemat(o)- is the combining form of hem(o)-, which the case study defines as blood.

questions.question: A patient's blood pressure reads 188/110 and is charted as hypertension. The prefix hyper- in that term means:
questions.explanation: The case study notes state that the prefix hyper- means "high," and combined with tension it refers to high blood pressure.

questions.question: A bleeding patient's blood pressure falls to 84/50 and he is described as hypotensive. The prefix hypo- tells you his blood pressure is:
questions.explanation: The case study uses hypo- to mean "low," as in hypoxia, low oxygen; here it makes hypotension low blood pressure.

questions.question: A paramedic starts an intravenous line for a patient who needs fluids. Knowing that intra- means "inside," the line delivers fluid:
questions.explanation: The case study explains that IV stands for intravenous, a fluid line placed inside a vein.

questions.question: An examiner documents weakness along the lateral side of a patient's arm. Based on latero-, the same word part in "lateral," the affected structures lie:
choices: Farther from the midline of the body
Closer to the midline of the body
questions.explanation: The flashcards define lateral as parts of the body that lie farther from the midline, also called outer structures.

questions.question: A hospital report shows that a nephrologist was consulted about a patient's failing kidneys. The word part nephro- tells you this specialist treats the:
questions.explanation: The case study breaks down nephrologist as nephr (kidney) plus -logist (specialist): a kidney specialist.

questions.question: A monitor shows supraventricular tachycardia. The prefix supra- tells you the abnormal electrical activity starts:
questions.explanation: The case study explains supraventricular tachycardia as a rapid heart rate whose electrical activity starts above (supra-) the ventricles.

questions.question: A resting patient's heart rate is 142 beats/min, charted as tachycardia. The prefix tachy- indicates the rate is:
questions.explanation: The case study defines tachy- as rapid in its breakdown of supraventricular tachycardia, a rapid heart rate.

questions.question: A patient's fingertips show a blue tint that is charted as cyanosis. The word part cyano- refers to the color:
questions.explanation: The case study breaks cyanosis down from cyan (blue) and -osis (condition): a blue skin color seen in hypoxia or poor perfusion.

questions.question: A lab report notes a low erythrocyte count. Knowing erythr/o- means "red" and -cyte means "cell," erythrocytes are the:
questions.explanation: The case study states that erythrocytes are the red blood cells, from erythro (red) and -cyte (cell); a low count means few red blood cells.

questions.question: Imaging reveals cardiomegaly in a patient with long-standing high blood pressure. The suffix -megaly tells you the heart is:
questions.explanation: The case study breaks down cardiomegaly as cardio (heart) plus -megaly (enlargement): an enlargement of the heart.

questions.question: A blood smear is examined for abnormal erythrocytes. The suffix -cyte in "erythrocyte" means:
questions.explanation: The case study gives -cyte as "cell" in its breakdown of erythrocyte, the red blood cell.

questions.question: A patient with respiratory distress sits bolt upright, saying he can breathe more easily that way, and his chart notes dyspnea. In this context, dyspnea means:
questions.explanation: In the case study the patient has respiratory distress and less dyspnea when placed in high-Fowler position on oxygen: dyspnea is difficulty breathing.

questions.question: After a hard coughing fit, a patient brings up blood from his airway. This finding is called:
questions.explanation: The case study defines hemoptysis as coughing up blood, from hemo, meaning blood.

questions.question: A patient has a long history of high blood pressure that is damaging his heart. This condition is called:
questions.explanation: The case study states that hyper- (high) combined with tension refers to high blood pressure: hypertension.

questions.question: A trauma patient's blood pressure drops to 82/48 after blood loss. This low blood pressure is termed:
questions.explanation: Hypo- means low, as the case study shows with hypoxia; low blood pressure is hypotension, the opposite of hypertension.

questions.question: A pulse oximeter reads 88% and your partner says to start treating the patient's hypoxia. Hypoxia is:
questions.explanation: The case study defines hypoxia directly: low oxygen, using the prefix hypo-, meaning low.

questions.question: An adult patient's resting heart rate is 138 beats/min. This rapid heart rate is called:
questions.explanation: Tachy- means rapid and cardi refers to the heart, so tachycardia is a rapid heart rate, as in the case study's supraventricular tachycardia at 130 beats/min.

questions.question: A patient has a laceration on the anterior surface of the abdomen. The anterior surface is the:
questions.explanation: The flashcards define anterior as the front surface of the body, the side facing you in the standard anatomic position.

questions.question: A fracture near the wrist is documented as a distal forearm fracture. Distal means the injury is:
choices: Farther from the trunk, nearer to the free end of the extremity
Closer to the trunk of the body
Closer to the midline of the body
Above the trunk of the body
questions.explanation: The flashcards define distal as farther from the trunk or nearer to the free end of the extremity.

questions.question: On an exam you note that the diaphragm lies inferior to the lungs. Inferior means it is positioned:
choices: Above the lungs, nearer to the head
Below the lungs, nearer to the feet
questions.explanation: The flashcards define inferior as below a body part or nearer to the feet.

questions.question: A patient points to pain on the lateral side of the knee. The lateral side is the:
choices: Inner side, closer to the midline
Outer side, farther from the midline
questions.explanation: The flashcards define lateral as parts of the body that lie farther from the midline, also called outer structures.

questions.question: A laceration is found on the medial side of the thigh. The medial side is the:
choices: Inner side, closer to the midline
Outer side, farther from the midline
questions.explanation: The flashcards define medial as parts of the body that lie closer to the midline, also called inner structures.

questions.question: Before transport, you check the patient's back for hidden injuries. The back surface of the body is called the:
questions.explanation: The flashcards define posterior as the back surface of the body, the side away from you in the standard anatomic position.

questions.question: A shoulder injury involves the proximal end of the humerus. Proximal means that end is:
questions.explanation: The flashcards define proximal as closer to the trunk.

questions.question: In the anatomic position, the head is superior to the neck. Superior means the head is:
choices: Below the neck, nearer to the feet
Above the neck, nearer to the head end of the body
questions.explanation: The flashcards define superior as above a body part or nearer to the head.

questions.question: You notice a blue tint to the fingers of both of a patient's hands, charted as bilateral cyanosis. Bilateral means the finding appears:
choices: On both sides of the midline
questions.explanation: The case study explains the patient has cyanosis bilaterally in his fingers, meaning both the right-sided and left-sided fingers; the flashcards define bilateral as appearing on both sides of the midline.

questions.question: A stroke patient reports weakness on one side of his body only. Weakness on one side is described as:
questions.explanation: The Assessment in Action keys unilateral as the term for "on one side," in contrast to bilateral, both sides.

questions.question: You arrive at a crash scene and find the patient lying face down on the ground. The patient is in the _____ position.
questions.explanation: The Assessment in Action and the flashcards both key prone as lying face down.

questions.question: For a full examination, you place the patient lying face up on the stretcher. This position is called:
questions.explanation: The flashcards define supine as lying face up, the opposite of prone, lying face down.

questions.question: A patient's chart reads "BP 156/94 mm Hg." The abbreviation BP stands for:
questions.explanation: The case study writes out "blood pressure (BP)" when giving the patient's vital signs.

questions.question: The monitor strip is annotated "HR 130 and irregular." The abbreviation HR refers to the patient's:
questions.explanation: The case study writes "heart rate (HR)" when reporting the patient's rate of 130 beats/min.

questions.question: A PCR lists HTN in the patient's past medical history. HTN means the patient has:
questions.explanation: The Assessment in Action and the case study both key HTN as the abbreviation for hypertension.

questions.question: A patient with abdominal pain points to the LLQ. The LLQ is the:
choices: Left upper quadrant of the abdomen
Left lower quadrant of the abdomen
Right lower quadrant of the abdomen
Right upper quadrant of the abdomen
questions.explanation: The flashcards define the quadrants as the four equal areas of the abdominal cavity divided at the umbilicus; LLQ names the left lower one.

questions.question: An abdominal exam documents tenderness in the LUQ. The LUQ is the:
choices: Left upper quadrant of the abdomen
Left lower quadrant of the abdomen
Right upper quadrant of the abdomen
Right lower quadrant of the abdomen
questions.explanation: Using the flashcards' definition of the abdominal quadrants, LUQ names the left upper quadrant.

questions.question: A chart notes RLQ pain in a patient being evaluated for appendicitis. The RLQ is the:
choices: Right upper quadrant of the abdomen
Right lower quadrant of the abdomen
Left lower quadrant of the abdomen
Left upper quadrant of the abdomen
questions.explanation: Using the flashcards' definition of the abdominal quadrants, RLQ names the right lower quadrant.

questions.question: A report documents RUQ tenderness after a fall. The RUQ is the:
choices: Right lower quadrant of the abdomen
Left upper quadrant of the abdomen
Right upper quadrant of the abdomen
Left lower quadrant of the abdomen
questions.explanation: Using the flashcards' definition of the abdominal quadrants, RUQ names the right upper quadrant.

questions.question: You treat a patient with oxygen at 12 L/min via an NRB. An NRB is a:
questions.explanation: The Assessment in Action scenario describes oxygen given at 12 L/min via a nonrebreathing mask, the device abbreviated NRB.

questions.question: After checking a patient's eyes, you chart PERRLA. PERRLA describes pupils that are:
choices: Equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation
questions.explanation: The Assessment in Action scenario describes the patient's pupils with the exact phrase PERRLA stands for: equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation.
